channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: The sleepy sickness in Vilhelmina—100-year-old mystery investigated
item.description: Researchers at CEDAR have studied and perhaps found an important piece in understanding one of the biggest medicinal mysteries of our time: the Sleepy Sickness that swept over Europe in the early 1900´s. During the 1920's, Sweden was one of the hardest-hit countries in the world, with the highest number of reported cases in Västerbotten, and especially the inland community of Vilhelmina.

item.title: Board game brings oral health inequalities research to life
item.description: A new board game developed by University of Liverpool researchers is creating opportunities for students, health professionals and other stakeholders to explore the social factors that influence oral health and access to dental care.

item.title: New analysis: Swedish aid for access to contraception saves women's lives
item.description: Swedish aid for modern contraceptives is estimated to have prevented 1.3 million unintended pregnancies and about 1,500 maternal deaths in low- and middle-income countries in 2024, according to a new analysis from Karolinska Institutet, the ONE Campaign and the Guttmacher Institute.

item.title: Cancer can evade immune attack by disrupting the teamwork of immune cells
item.description: The immune system's attack on cancer depends on more than cells capable of killing tumors. It also requires a coordinated effort in which some immune cells recognize danger, rally reinforcements and help train other components in a vast disease-fighting network.

item.title: Artificial protein activates faulty insulin receptors and lowers blood sugar in mice
item.description: The body relies on a finely tuned network of receptors that unlock their docking sites in response to specific chemical signals. In some genetic diseases, however, mutations can leave these receptors unable to do their job. A recent study published in Science Translational Medicine has offered a way around this problem with an artificial protein designed to activate one such mutated receptor.

item.title: mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute
item.description: Trials of an experimental Ebola vaccine aimed at the strain behind the current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have begun in neighboring Uganda, its virus research institute said Friday.

item.title: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
item.description: For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

item.title: A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes
item.description: In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins.

item.title: Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism
item.description: For many people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ordinary sensory experiences can be unusually intense or overwhelming. A light touch or a mildly uncomfortable sensation may provoke a disproportionately strong response, making everyday activities difficult.

item.title: PROLIFIC risk score made publicly available to pulmonary fibrosis researchers
item.description: The Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation and Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC) have published a paper in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine detailing the development and validation of the PROLIFIC Risk Score, a novel blood biomarker-based tool designed to predict disease progression in people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

item.title: Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
item.description: People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

item.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
item.description: Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

item.title: Does drinking raw milk actually deliver extra health benefits? Here's the science
item.description: The popularity of raw milk in Google searches and Instagram post topics has soared over the past 10 years, spurred on by influencers claiming there are benefits to consuming raw milk.

item.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be due to your blood sugar and genes
item.description: Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

item.title: Brainstem atlas reveals possible REM sleep center in humans
item.description: During REM sleep, we dream and our muscles relax into a temporary paralysis called atonia. People with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder—or iRBD—lack atonia, causing them to shout or violently move their arms and legs during REM sleep. This disorder may also be an early symptom of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's or dementia with Lewy bodies, as many people with iRBD later develop these disorders.

item.title: Should you correct a friend's health myth? Ask yourself this question first
item.description: "You must drink eight glasses of water a day" is the kind of advice a friend might offer. But what the advice leaves out is that our daily fluid intake comes from a variety of sources, including other drinks and food.

item.title: Liver protein as a potential biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
item.description: A key factor in identifying a biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) is understanding whether there are biological differences between treatment-resistant and non-treatment-resistant patients. Approximately 25% of all schizophrenia patients do not respond to medication. To better treat these patients, scientists at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry (MPIP) collected comprehensive data on cell distributions and proteins from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples taken from patients with and without TRS. When they compared these concentrations with those in the blood, they found elevated levels of the protein albumin in the CSF.

item.title: New approach could make curative lung cancer treatment possible for more patients
item.description: Despite significant advances in treatment, lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. A clinical trial recently published in Nature Medicine suggests that a more flexible approach to treating locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer could open up new treatment options for patients. By starting with a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy (durvalumab), followed by reassessment by a multidisciplinary team, doctors may be able to offer curative surgery to more patients. The study also suggests that patients who remain ineligible for surgery after this initial treatment may still have another potentially curative option: a combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

item.title: Dreaming of better sleep? Personalized mathematical modeling may help turn that dream into reality
item.description: It's something we're all familiar with—the frustration of a bad night's sleep. But what is a bad night's sleep, exactly? For some, it might look like lying awake, being unable to fall asleep. For others, sleep may come quickly, only to be interrupted by unwanted early-morning wake-ups.

item.title: How to recognize when video gaming becomes an addiction
item.description: Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

item.title: Existing drug helps mice clear blood through meningeal lymphatic system after stroke
item.description: A drug already used to improve blood circulation and prevent certain types of stroke could have an unexpected new role in promoting recovery after bleeding in the brain. In a study published in Stroke, a team led by researchers at National Taiwan University found that cilostazol helped mice recover from intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) by boosting the brain's natural drainage system.

item.title: Living wound patch pairs viruses and probiotics to fight resistant bacteria
item.description: Antibiotic-resistant germs are one of the greatest threats to our health. As the existing arsenal of antibiotics loses its effectiveness, even routine treatments can become considerably more risky. This "silent pandemic" is exacerbated by the ability of microorganisms to form biofilms. These extremely tenacious accumulations of germs can become a particular problem in hospitals. Antibiotics and disinfectants can hardly penetrate these films. In addition, biofilms promote the further spread of antibiotic resistance to other bacteria.

item.title: An RNA therapy approach to treat heart damage in Fabry disease
item.description: Fabry disease, also known as Morbus Fabry, is an inherited metabolic disorder in which certain fatty substances cannot be broken down sufficiently. These substances then accumulate in various organs, where they can cause serious damage.

item.title: Learning a new movement may start with a reusable pattern
item.description: A signature can remain recognizable when someone writes it with their non-dominant other hand, even though different muscles have produced it. Such flexibility hints at an internal pattern for an action that can be reused in different circumstances. But does that pattern emerge only after years of practice, or can it help us learn from the start?

item.title: The littlest and cutest research subjects help explain infant brains
item.description: Every new parent knows the difficulty of trying to get a newborn to sleep. Northeastern University researchers have an added challenge: getting a newborn to sleep during a brain scan.

item.title: Bootleg nicotine could warp Australia's smoking trends
item.description: After decades of effort to curb smoking rates, the black market for tobacco and vapes has exploded in Australia in the last five years.

item.title: Ebola data from West Africa suggest potential benefit of the antidiarrheal drug loperamide
item.description: Ebola virus disease causes severe diarrhea and vomiting in the majority of affected patients. In resource-limited settings, some patients receive the antidiarrheal agent loperamide during the early stages of illness, when oral intake remains possible. An international research team has now systematically evaluated the potential benefit of this treatment strategy for Ebola patients for the first time.

item.title: What do puberty's wild hormone swings mean for teenage girls' mental health?
item.description: Behind the stereotype of the moody teenager is a far more complex picture: fluctuating hormones, emotional swings and a brain in the middle of major renovations.

item.title: Brain's myelin 'brake' may hold clues to mental health disorders
item.description: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers have identified a cellular "brake" that helps prevent excessive myelin growth in the brain, which has been linked to mental health conditions such as major depressive disorder, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

item.title: Aged care move disrupts regular health care
item.description: Moving into residential aged care can disrupt long-standing relationships with doctors and other health care providers, highlighting the need for stronger handover processes to protect continuity of care for older Australians, experts say.
